items.text: I'm in a similar vein to Misti. Some people may love Cirque shows, and still hate Le Reve (which is it's own separate discussion). What I loved about Le Reve is the theater, and its design. The set and decorations are beautiful start to finish, and its concept is beautiful and charming. Unfortunately it doesn't translate well. Live it's not very entertaining. When I saw a showing, it malfunctions kept happening all night which made it hard to enjoy certain bits, even good ones. It's going for the flashy Cirque experience, and never really gets there. What I think it's worth seeing mostly for the theater. Otherwise it's something you'd be better off spending on something else.

Picked this up used mechanical at $38. Its about $38 of keyboard or at least close. Space bar rattles. Every time I hit my thumbs, it clatters hollow like a tray of cutlery. During work I stop hearing the rattle. But past midnight that noise really stands out. I just type around it. The E key repeats too, so I type "meeeting" instead of "meeting". Once a couple times, maybe once every 3 or 4 paragraphs. Rare enough to forget and often enough that I read everything carefully before sending it. Messaged seller what switch it was, was too lazy to wait. Bought it and after a week it said brown switches. Keeping it because this is good. Every key has a bump partway through. Means my fingers know when a press registers and never slam it down to bottom. I get through email at 6 or 7 pages, not feeling bad in my wrists. The laptop never did this. Thought about returning it, the shipping would eat up a lot of what I paid. Plus would be on my laptop. So I keep it.

The theater and stage are both circular. This gives every seat a good view and helps with that storyline, which is hard to follow. During big transitions, the show really leans on 3 main entrances. The performers are very talented with incredible strength and aerobic ability. All of us watched them breath hold for mins at a time. The theater and lighting and whole setting was really pretty. The music wasn't always well suited for the movements and some seemed dull. My take on the quality of the show is very good and recommend, but I'd take away one star because of the story and tunes. In terms of price in the Vegas context (compared to O and Love) they're pretty reasonable. I wanted more special effects, more flame stuff or something. But I think that it is entertaining to watch. It's not a serious drawback that we have it that way.

Everyone treats remote work like the cure-all. After a couple of years of mentoring five junior engineers I'm convinced it's overhyped for juniors who are just learning the craft. Junior developers aren't really after tickets and docs or even meetings, but they have to go into design discussions, to see how others go about debugging a problem. They have to feel comfortable raising queries before wasting hours on confusion. That sort of exchange takes place as it occurs in offices. To make remote work work for them, you need to be at ease with when is reasonable, setting up a call, and describing an issue they don't fully understand. This is a very challenging skill to have without a way to learn it. In actual remote work, code review's short comments have felt like the end of debate, rather than a chance to learn. And things take longer, therefore less momentum. In the five junior people I coached, I saw them progressing more rapidly with pairing work side by side, whiteboard sessions, and easy communication with people with more knowledge. Its not me being pro-office or anti-flex. Remote work works well for self-driven devs. But as far as juniors go, working in close vicinity is like a booster. You get more confidence, context, and instincts. Sending a junior to remote with just a computer and a calendar schedule is like a drag on a junior's learning and can be the source of less well technical leadership in the future.

So at 3:17 am the mixer had this low drone going through my boots, and flour was floating through the air, all lit up by this harsh fluorescent. Dough loaves were resting on wooden boards, crusts really soft and pale, not ready for their final bake. I wiped my hands on my apron, apron stiff with all that dry dough and sweat. I moved to the counter to check the lock, which really is a paranoia ritual more than anything practical, not like any need. The book was still there, The History of Salt, a blue hardback, it's spine cracked at the top. There every Thursday for six weeks now; it sits in the same spot by the front counter, on that glass case above the still unsold cinnamon rolls. It doesn't really belong there. The bakery is not a branch of the municipal library system. Anyway I picked it up. It was cold. I wanted it open for a forgotten mark, or the blankness. But a square piece of notebook paper was folded inside, and slipped out, on the counter with a soft thump.

I looked at the handwriting. The pen is really pressed hard into the fiber. I could see: use left hand to knead; don't lean on the right; it damages the tension. He looked at his left hand, red-knuckled and covered in flour white. He put it back. He closed it, put it back on the glass case, and aligned it perfectly. He then turned off the overhead above the display case, leaving it in shadow.

I think apple deserves a mention here, my personal experience. My school only allowed apple computers for middle and high schoolers. They were expensive, costed double compared to pc laptops. They were super unreliable, broke every month or so. Never once dropped my laptop, but I had it replace the HDD like five times in four years, reinstalled the os multiple times. One of the extreme cases. A friends macbook pro literally caught on fire while he was watching a movie, smoke alarm going off. Apple support was useless, I could spend hours on the phone with them. They never diagnosed the problem, just backup, wipe and restore files. My gripe also extends to the iphones, I had the first iphone, it was very flaky. These days apple is releasing a new iphone almost every two months. And its really just camera improvements. So just a slightly better camera compared to the last generation. Only good: ipad, i will concede its the best tablet out there for now, but android tablets will get better soon.

*Awakening* at the Wynn is fine but not a must see to build a trip around. I grew up visiting Vegas and I’ve seen a lot of shows before i was 21. And therefore i have a reference. Good news. The stage is circular. You can see it nicely basically from anywhere, which is rare for these kind of big theater shows. Also, if you stay in Wynn or Encore, tickets that are normally $125 are $99. Which helps. Some individual acts are impressive. Performers are good for sure (aerialists, acrobats etc). But the problem is the story. And for a show, it’s really lacking. Its kind of unclear and weak or doesn’t even really exist. I did not get what it was for, it was too much. So, all of the feats you see here, I saw in Cirque du Soleil. Not the best maybe. But they’re just doing the same tricks. There’s too many bits going on. Like it needs to back off. There’s too many stunts, and then too many visuals. Too many “wow things” in the show. Maybe less would work here. But outside of some cool stunts, it feels pretty average. Nothing blew me away. The people who went with me? None of them seemed blown away or overwhelmed or anything. But some of my friends did enjoy it. If you haven’t seen this show maybe see it, especially if you have the hotel deal. But i wouldn’t see again. Or pay for full price, like $125+. I really just think that it’s more of a stereotypical Vegas big flash show that the more, the better. But more was more messy, to me.

My friend, his younger brother and I went back to Zumiez to pick the remaining board-related stuff. At first, everything seemed fine. We chatted with a female employee while she assembled the skateboard. Introduced herself as a manager, claimed that throughout her employment she was assembling them every day. That one day when she had a bad day and was feeling annoyed that's when she was mistreating people or customers. She took approx. 90 minutes while we expected it to not be more than 15 minutes to assemble. She stripped two bolts on the skateboard, then she replaced them in a manner that it seemed they are going to be reused and sold to another customer. In order to finish or assist her brother who was described by her as a manager, another employee brought in. No apology for wasting our time. To us it feels like the skateboard was used and we want our future business back. Zumiez has lost us. My heart is broken.

I got this mechanical keyboard used just for thirty eight dollars, and it's been a chaotic ride if somewhat good. The guys I bought it from had very bad communication. I had sent them a message to ask what type of switch is in the keyboard, took about one week to reply with a one line answer by which time I had already bought it on a gamble. The board itself is also well loved, the spacebar has extremely annoying rattle like loose lego in it, e key sometimes double type, so my emails get hilarious typos theee instead of the. However, I do love typing on it. The feedback is very nice and feels great for typing long ass work emails. I even thought of returning it in the beginning but it's more hassle than to ship a slab of plastic $38 keyboard to them. And I stuck to it so have grown to like it more. But if you don't mind a bit of diy tuning, occasional double typewrite e and like some minor adjustments, it's a winner for its budget price.

A float valve controls the trough filling. There's a buoyant float on a valve. The water level drops then the float drops, it opens the valve to let water in. When the water starts rising, then float starts rising too to close the valve slowly. When it reaches the set level then valve closes off, and it's done filling. When it overflows, that typically happens for two reasons. There's either some grunge in there or some mineral buildup, and it just cannot close completely, or the float is not set right, the float's too high, the float closes the valve at the point where it's already overflowing.

Ken Lay has sent an email to all Enron employees. The days have been difficult given problems inside Enron and what’s happening in the world, so the holiday season doesn’t feel much like a holiday. It’s been talked about a lot internally about whether they hold the all-Enron holiday party scheduled December 8. People felt differently. Some thought it’d be a good chance for Enron employees to come together and celebrate. Others felt it wasn’t appropriate right now. Then it was decided to cancel the party. Spending company funds on celebration at this moment would easily be seen as imprudent, a risk they didn’t want to take. I’m sorry. You’ve all worked hard and deserve a reason to celebrate and recognition, and they’ll look for more suitable ways to recognize outstanding contributions during the holiday season.

Siphons work by moving liquid from one container to another, which is higher than the other container. Its use is not just to make it easier to pour water out of a bottle, but more specifically it is for transporting or draining water. Water flows down from the first container through the down leg, and if this goes low enough, it pulls water through the up leg, and so you can siphon it into another container. But if the air breaks that water column, then it breaks the vacuum inside the down leg, and all equalizes out with the pressure of the other container. So if any air bubbles in, it stops it. So that's the trick. You have to fill the tube with water so there's no air in it. You can then use a siphon to transfer liquids. So you put the siphon in the upper reservoir, let the water fall down and it will create a vacuum, the pressure will then push water in and it will flow down until it's at the same height as the source. If the water level in the upper reservoir falls below the top of the tube, the water breaks the vacuum.

A copy of The Count of Monte Cristo showed up again, as usual, on top of the flour bin. It was always on Thursdays, and this one had the Richmond Public Library stamp. The sourdough was on its second rise and I found it. I never see anyone go in through the screen door even though it creaks and squeaks like crazy. I think because around 3am I am mostly yeast in my head with caffeine, so I hear things, I just can't see them, and I don't look out the windows. Tonight I found a piece of legal paper sticking out of the novel like a bookmark. So, I wiped my hands on my apron and it left a smudge on it, white on black, but it didn't really matter. And the note was like 'Please, watch page 142'. It was really scratchy, spiky writing, not a cursive font. And it was in pencil. And it said 'I think they're watching the drop-boxes now'. Then I felt a draught blow through the kitchen. It smelled like rain, wet asphalt. But I just didn't open the book. But I carefully put the note back, wrapped the book in a pastry bag, and I folded it to make it fit and seal it.

I paid thirty-eight dollars for this used mechanical keyboard, and honestly I think it was worth those bucks, maybe just a hair more, no more. It's a used product so it's gonna have its quirks. I've been using a laptop keyboard for about a year which is much flatter. So, the quirks are... The main flaw is the spacebar just rattle. The spacebar just rattles on every hit of thumb, very rattle. I've stopped noticing it during the day. It's more like late at night it's kinda loud, much louder than it should be. It's like... a tray of cutlery being hit a bunch of times. So that's annoying. The other flaw, the E key repeats itself. Like, instead of typing "meeting" it will type something like "meeeting". The repeats aren't frequent, maybe every few paragraphs, or less frequent than that, but often enough to make me proofread.

I also had a hard time communication with the seller. I asked about the switches before I bought it and it took a full week to get an answer after I bought it and after the keyboard arrived. They're brown switches. And here's the good part, which is a pleasant surprise for the price: it's pretty comfortable. It has a cushioned feel and is great for typing emails for longer emails. You just sit there and type and your wrists aren't complaining. So I actually considered sending it back, but decided it's fine as it works, and the hassle wasn't worth it. So it's on my desk. And now it's just staying here as is. So it works fine, it's comfortable, it rattles, it repeats, it does what's asked of it, and does not really annoy me. So for me it works, and it works as I wanted it to, and it has earned it, and I'm keeping it. So it's three stars.

Old school attendance registers let historians dig into the patterns of daily life not found in formal records. If people want to know, registers can explain why a child showed or did not and if it was weather, health, work needed, and family problems. The register can also show gender gap and how schooling fit into daily life and how a child was involved in the family routines. But with registers you need to remember registers are just the record, what teachers want to note. If you study them many years in a row you can actually see trends of education change and public health trends. But they are limited, what they say is not necessarily true, teachers might not report all children or report absences and be missing some notes on what their absences were, and teachers might see or not see a child present as their own thoughts or observations and they do not ask the children. So you want compare with other evidence, and then they really are useful.

Mara would leave the back door unlocked at 2:17 each Thursday morning. The same book every time, a moth identification manual on the bakery's rear step. Ghost pale county sticker on the spine, and flour ground down into the jacket. As if the book was actually helping in this. She'd sent it back twice to the libranirans, they just smiled too polite so for week 3 she'd just kept it next to her rye starter and said nothing.

Tonight, rain ticked on the alley door, ovens were breathing and she was forming croissants, her palm pressing the butter into the dough, then the latch clicked, small and guilty.

Just the book. Dry as a bone on the wet concrete. Now she wiped her apron open up the page, found a scrap of paper slipped between Luna Moth and Promethea, folded once.

I'm sorry about the crumbs. Your window is the only light on this street. I read it till the first bus came.

She looked to the alley and saw dent milk crates, and steam coming from the drains, at that second, the city felt enormous, then it didn't. Tore a little corner of her order pad and wrote: Cinnamon rolls at 4:05, then just put the note in the book, put the book on a warm windowsill. Back door unlock.

As the assignment says, we were testing these bridge designs and seeing what could hold, or hold better, more weight. So in our group we decided to make two types of these bridge designs. We made it as standard size as possible. One of them is triangular-shaped folds, one of them is arch-shaped. And then one of them is sort of just beam, like just flat board with no other shapes. And what we did is that we put two supports and put this bridge on top of them. And then we put some weights and saw how it would bend or topple over or fall apart. We couldn't test under controlled conditions, like what we did with cardboard. And we couldn't make our models completely identical, we made them as consistent size as we could. But since it's done with our hands, it's kind of limited. So these results are not engineering results. In our classroom activity the triangular folds appear to hold more weight, and the others were more unstable.

Marguerite found the book lying on the steel table by the back door. Or rather, it wasn't really lying there, it was under the bench, the one by the back door where the bread peels hang. Book is called a field guide to coastal birds. Cover had Harbor Street branch stamp inside with a due date, March. It had been lost for eleven Thursdays. The mail slot in that door is nailed shut and the hatch, the flour man's hatch, is just a little bit broken. No latch really. She asked staff, she checked hatch for scratches, she stayed till 4pm with her jacket on once. Nothing. So one day it's 3pm, 2 or 4pm, 3pm, and she was always at the ovens, not facing door, and it did come. And tonight there's a grocery bag, a receipt from Pell's, stuck inside the book, folded up, on the page of the oystercatcher. And it's, the writing on the receipt was very scratched, the pen had worn out. I keep meaning to return this to the library, but I go in front of your door and smell the bread smell and I put it down, can stop if you want. So Marguerite smelled salt, who it was. She pulled a pencil from her apron and wrote, on the back of the receipt. Bring it Thursday, I'll have a roll. She put in her roll, she left it on the hatch, a warm roll, on a plate.

I live in Toronto now and don't use Hydro Ottawa any more. And because of what happened, I do feel pretty compelled to warn folks. A lot happened. So, this is my experience. It's my experience.
I had an account with them for a year as I was living in a downtown apartment while I studied. Then I moved home to do my masters with my parents, so I cancelled the account, paid everything, was done and went home.
And they kept taking money from my bank account for more than a year at random times and amounts. So I phone them a lot of times but no one seems to fix it. All I did was send them screenshots of the payments they were randomly withdrawing and just kept insisting the account was closed and no debit charges were being made to my account. And it took me several years or months just to get to a manager, and a manager then finally addressed it. After many hours on the phone with many different customer service reps, a manager finally went into this properly, looked up my account and found that they had linked my banking information to the account number of my parents because, well, I was moving home and it should not have linked it automatically. My parents only found out because I went through all of their bills and saw something weird. My parents said, oh, I feel like these are always in the plus, we have always been overpaying, we were always getting money back.
After all these things, so much effort, the manager admitted the problem was fixed. But initially refused to refund all the charges or at least part of the charges. They only offered an apology. So I guess I've learned my lesson. I'll never offer up my bank details to them or anyone at face value and just hope for the best, not going to do it again, and they just really need to get their act together. The way they mishandle your personal information really should be alarming.

Marisol was proofing a second batch of rye around 3:40 AM when that other book showed up again. The book on flour bins by the back door, the plastic jacket of the book is cold from being in the alley.

Its been this book every 4th Thursday. The book has been stamped Eastgate Branch but its been due for three weeks already. Every Thursday, on the way home I have to carry it to the drop box. But then it ends up coming back as if the building borrowed it.

She wiped her hands on her apron, opened the book on barn owls, and found a little index card folded inside. It was a handwritten note that read this:

The person says "You're leaving vent fan on it is 5 am I smell bread in the alley". Then "I walk my mothers dog now because she can't do it anymore". Then "I keep forgetting to return. May be I want to not". Signed R.

Marisol read this card twice. The timer in the oven is counting down. The vent fan hums and is putting a little air in the alley.

The card has another note on it, written with grease pencil, the same pencil you would use on an oven to mark trays or something. "Rye's out at 4:15". She tears off the heel of yesterday's loaf of bread, wraps it in wax paper, sets the book on top of the box, and opens the back door one inch.

I used Ryanair as a poor student with my ex in Sweden, so it was the cheap option. Awful trip. At the airport my £20 bottle of L’Occitane shower gel was confiscated and they said it was over the liquid limit even when it wasnt over. Then they said I could go to the pharmacy and get it back if i bought a 100ml bottle of the same shower gel there. So I did that, paid, went back and said I bought a bottle, and nobody knew what I was talking about. £20 gone and I was mad. They also charged me another £5 at the gate because I had a bottle of water in my carry-on even though I bought it in the airport. So they charged me £5, which felt really stupid to me. So, Ryanair has now stopped doing LPL-Stockholm-Skavsta so I now use Norwegian air. Norwegian is also a bad customer service, funny in a way. But at least their planes are newer, less antiqued.

So this isn't unique; I had one of those rain hits on Tuesday. And then on Thursday, about half of my Brandywine vines split. On the fruit you can see a seam, it runs down the side of it. Same thing happens all the time. Long time dry and then the weather dumps rain all at once. And the inside of the fruit takes water so fast that the skin can't keep up. The Sungolds are holding up mostly fine for now but a few do look like they might be the same.

And once it happens, can't help or prevent it. But you know, what can help to a degree is you've already got that two day schedule. And just even out the amount of water that you are putting on a daily or weekly or whatever time frequency. But ultimately it won't help in this storm. Probably you get pretty good crop from the rest of it. And the ones that are split, just pick them and put them to some other use. The Brandywine is going to be more work, as opposed to the Sungold. But they've got those skins, thick skins that they can't stretch. And it'll be more work to clean it all up once it happens. And you're just hoping to not be affected the same way with the Sungolds. Can limit the amount of rain they get in one shot.

My friend wrote an SAT Subject Test an hour long, but proctoring mistake they got an extra twenty minutes on top. She's a very integrity minded person and because it was an unfair advantage, it made the test not standardized or anything, so she used their official hotline to report it. And you know what? It was total institutional injustice. And they did their investigation and said, oh, there was insufficient evidence of the improprieties so we won't hold the proctor, we won't hold the students in the room. But then they also said, there was evidence of impropriety by my friend, so we're going to cancel her scores. So it's punishing the whistleblower, the person who brought the issue to light and excusing the real violation. And that just shows how badly, how unjustly, how broken the College Board is really.

So Thursdays, this book shows up. But not at the counter. It sits wedged behind the flour bins by the back door. Whoever leaves it knows the spot won't trip me up.

It is always the same book: A Field Guide to North American Moths. From the Elmwood branch. It's been borrowed so long ago that the ink on the returned due date is purple. Nobody has ever seen anyone put the book down. At about 2am I am elbow deep in rye dough, and honestly at that time I wouldn't notice a marching band.

For the first few weeks, I would put it on the shelf next to the till. But by Saturday morning it was gone. And Thursdays, it showed up again. Fine. People were a bit weird like this. But I'm the type to talk to his sourdough starter so who am I to judge?

Tonight there was a note stuck on page 114. About luna moth pages, and it says luna moths barely live a week and don't even eat. So I always think how is this a waste of a beautiful creature. Do you ever get to see the bread before it's gone. There's no signature. It's just some pencil lines. And they were written pretty heavy.

So I just read it over. Three times, and the sound of oven ticking out loud. And when we pulled the very first bread of the night, it was hot and crackling, and I wrapped it in brown paper and placed it behind the flour bins.

Its stuffiness has little to do with just temperature. High humidity keeps that moist feeling on your skin. Low airflow, bad ventilation, and a lack of air movement makes it feel very close and heavy. It makes air feel stale. The air conditioning can lower the temperature or maybe lower the humidity, but a lot of the time it just lowers the temperature. It does not necessarily mean you have good airflow. So that stuffy feeling will still be there and the heat and the carbon dioxide will stick around. Opening the windows or using a fan and ventilation gets you a bit fresh, or at least it improves the feeling.

Everyone says remote work benefits everybody. But I have spent the past two years mentoring five junior engineers and this is not a win for all. Junior people learn very differently from how you might learn. For them it is a matter of sitting in on the discussions, design arguments, and bug fixing, and getting answers, rather than going off on their own. This is easy to do in an office. But it is hard to do remotely, for them. What it comes down to is, for a junior engineer, it is very easy for them to lose direction when they are remote. It gets confusing.

So we get very poor feedback, for example, from remote code reviews. They end up reading like a judgement, and it is very hard to have a conversation with somebody. So you just end up losing momentum. I have seen junior engineers who were working in the office and pair-programming together on a white board or with the senior engineer for example, move along much faster than if you just hand them a laptop. But none of this means you scrap the flexibility of remote. This works great if it is a mid to senior person who will be able to direct themselves. For a beginner, it is a different story.

The confidence, context, and judgement to be a good software engineer come from being around senior people. And if you just hand them a laptop and a calendar in a remote-only setting, you will end up with weaker technical leadership over time.

Rain is just measured like this. Rain falls into the gauge, which is just a tube. What happens to all of the water that falls into the gauge. It's got a scale down the side. They make the gauge opening smaller in the top so it doesn't collect too much, then has a very slim tube that the water then goes into. The scale is calibrated to compensate for the ratio of the areas. And so what the gauge tells you is just how deep a flat ground would be if it didn't sink in, or evaporate or drain off. So what you get is a rainfall amount of how much rainfall we've had in millimeters. Wind can be an error, because when wind blows around the gauge it will blow the raindrops past and undercount on the gauge. Or if it's just sitting there, you've got evaporation or splashes off.

School attendance registers can be extremely useful to historians. They help us build pictures of communities in past eras. We see the shape of school life and local life from this. For example, attendance can drop off in certain places and this suggests that in some communities that children need to harvest crops on the farm. Or we can see drops that correspond with epidemics or very poor weather conditions which we know from weather reports or newspapers. We can also see certain groups missing more often than others, which suggests to us that in that era, in that community, there were underlying cultural beliefs. But these kinds of registers really only work really well if the records are accurate. And of course there is the problem of manipulation, where a teacher or headmaster may manipulate records to get through or meet requirements. Or it can be that they're making things up, or they don't know why a child is missing, they just put down absent. We really know why they're missing from other sources. So for us to have a true representation of school life and local life, we have to cross reference other evidence with this data.

I'm gonna talk about a float valve in a drink water for cattle because this is actually very common stuff, but not widely known. So a float valve connects the trough to a pressurized water line, there's a buoyant float which is a plastic ball or block usually and that float sits on the surface of the water inside the trough and attached to a lever. So as the cattle drink from the trough the water level lowers, lowers, so the float sinks and the float tilts the lever arm which pulls the plunger or washer away from the seat in the valve. So as the water lowers the arm pulls the plunger away and the water comes in to fill up the trough. But as the water goes up the float goes up with it. And as the float goes up, the lever pushes the plunger or washer back onto the seat, gradually closing the hole until it reaches the set level. So when you have an overflow issue in a water trough, it's either the washer is worn out or dirty, has debris stuck on it so it can't close and the water keeps flowing into the valve. Or your float is punctured or water logged, waterlogged and it doesn't lift up as far so it can't close.
